title: Tooth types, shapes & functions
blurb: Incisors, canines, premolars and molars: how each is shaped, how many roots it has and what it is built to do.
question: The dentist is about to extract an upper first molar and asks you to lay out the forceps. A student nurse asks why upper molar forceps have a pointed beak on one side when lower molar forceps have points on both. What do you need to know about molar roots to explain it?

teach.body: Humans have four types of teeth, each shaped for a different stage of eating. Incisors at the front cut food. Canines at the corners grip and tear. Premolars behind them start crushing, and molars at the back grind food ready to swallow. The front six teeth in each arch (incisors and canines) are called anterior teeth; premolars and molars are posterior teeth. Shape follows function: the further back a tooth sits, the broader its biting surface and the more roots it usually has.

teach.caption: Root numbers are the usual pattern. Variations are common, especially in third molars.
In every quadrant, counting from the midline: 1 and 2 are incisors, 3 is the canine (highlighted), 4 and 5 are premolars, 6, 7 and 8 are molars.

teach.body: Incisors have a thin, straight incisal edge for slicing into food, a single root and no true cusps. Newly erupted incisors often show three small bumps on the edge (mamelons) that wear away. Canines have one strong pointed cusp and the longest roots in the mouth, the upper canine longest of all. That long root anchors them firmly, so canines are often among the last teeth lost and make good bridge or denture abutments. They also support the corners of the lips, which is why losing them changes facial appearance.

Premolars usually have two cusps (one buccal, one lingual), which is why they are also called bicuspids; the lower second premolar often has three. Most have one root, but the upper first premolar usually has two (buccal and palatal). Molars have broad occlusal surfaces with four or five cusps separated by fissures. Upper molars usually have three roots: two buccal (mesiobuccal and distobuccal) and one palatal. Lower molars usually have two: mesial and distal. Where roots divide is called the furcation.

teach.caption: Right: a molar with a broad occlusal surface, several cusps separated by fissures, and more than one root. Left: a narrower, two-rooted tooth seen from the side. Broad, ridged chewing surfaces are built for grinding.

teach.caption: Forceps beaks are shaped to sit into the furcation, so the root pattern decides which forceps you lay out.
8 + 4 + 8 + 12 = 32 permanent teeth. The deciduous set has no premolars and only 2 molars per quadrant: 20 teeth.

teach.text: There are NO deciduous premolars. Permanent premolars erupt in place of the deciduous MOLARS. And remember the root rule: UPPER molars have THREE roots (two buccal, one palatal), LOWER molars have TWO (mesial and distal).

items: Incisors cut (incisal edge, 1 root); canines tear (1 cusp, longest root).
Premolars crush (usually 2 cusps, 1 root; upper first premolar usually 2 roots).
Molars grind (4 or 5 cusps; upper 3 roots, lower 2 roots).
Anterior = incisors + canines; posterior = premolars + molars.

summary: You can now name the four tooth types, describe the shape and job of each, state the usual number of cusps and roots, and use the upper versus lower molar root pattern to explain why different extraction forceps are needed.

A.q: Which tooth type is shaped mainly for gripping and tearing food?
A.why: Canines have a single strong pointed cusp and a long root, ideal for gripping and tearing.

whyNot.0: Incisors have a thin incisal edge for cutting and biting.
whyNot.1: Premolars have two cusps for crushing food.
whyNot.2: Molars have broad surfaces for grinding.

A.q: How many roots does an upper first permanent molar usually have?
A.why: Upper molars usually have three roots: mesiobuccal, distobuccal and palatal.

whyNot.0: A single root is typical of incisors, canines and most premolars.
whyNot.1: Two roots (mesial and distal) is the usual pattern for lower molars.
whyNot.3: Four roots is not the usual pattern for any permanent tooth.

A.q: Which teeth are classed as anterior teeth?
A.why: The anterior teeth are the six front teeth in each arch: four incisors and two canines.

whyNot.1: Premolars are posterior teeth, even though they sit next to the canines.
whyNot.2: Premolars and molars together make up the posterior teeth.
whyNot.3: Premolars are posterior, so this pairing mixes the two groups.

B.q: Which permanent tooth usually has the longest root in the mouth?
B.why: The upper canine has the longest root of any tooth, which anchors it firmly.

whyNot.0: Upper central incisors have a single root, but it is shorter than the canine's.
whyNot.2: Lower first molars have two roots, each much shorter than a canine root.
whyNot.3: The upper first premolar usually has two fairly short roots.

B.q: A student says premolars are found in both dentitions. What is the correct response?
B.why: There are no deciduous premolars. The eight permanent premolars erupt in place of the deciduous molars.

whyNot.0: Deciduous teeth have molars in that position, not premolars.
whyNot.1: Only the permanent set has premolars; the deciduous set has none.
whyNot.3: The deciduous dentition has no premolars at all.

B.q: Which permanent tooth usually has two roots, one buccal and one palatal?
B.why: The upper first premolar is the premolar that usually has two roots, buccal and palatal.

whyNot.1: Lower premolars usually have a single root.
whyNot.3: Lower molars usually have two roots, but they are mesial and distal, not buccal and palatal.

C.q: What is the main function of the incisors?
C.why: Incisors have a chisel-like incisal edge for cutting and biting into food.

whyNot.0: Grinding is the job of the molars.
whyNot.1: Tearing is the job of the canines.
whyNot.2: Crushing is mainly done by the premolars.

C.q: The dentist asks for lower molar forceps. Why do their beaks have a point on BOTH sides?
options: Lower molars have one conical root
Lower molars have three separate roots
They fit a buccal and lingual furcation
The beaks grip the crown, not the root
C.why: Lower molars have mesial and distal roots, so there is a furcation on both the buccal and lingual sides for the beaks to engage.

whyNot.0: Lower molars usually have two roots, not one.
whyNot.1: Three roots is the upper molar pattern.
whyNot.3: Forceps beaks are designed to grip the root area, not just the crown.

C.q: How many molars are there in a full permanent dentition?
C.why: There are three molars in each quadrant (first, second and third), so 3 x 4 = 12.

whyNot.0: Eight is the number of permanent incisors, or of premolars.
whyNot.2: Ten is not a correct count for any permanent tooth type.
whyNot.3: Sixteen would mean four molars per quadrant.

reteach.title: Your teeth are a kitchen knife block
reteach.question: Think about the tools you use to prepare a meal. Which tooth matches which tool, and why does the shape suit the job?

blocks.body: Incisors are the knives: thin, sharp edges for slicing into an apple. Canines are the meat hooks: one strong point with a deep anchor (the longest root) for gripping and tearing. Premolars are the nutcrackers: two cusps that start crushing. Molars are the pestle and mortar: wide, bumpy surfaces that grind food to paste. The harder the job, the more roots the tooth needs to stay put, which is why molars have two or three.

blocks.h: Food's journey from front to back

explain.body: Two per quadrant (central and lateral). A thin, straight incisal edge cuts food. One root each. Together with the canines they are the anterior teeth.

test.q: Which feature is typical of an incisor?
test.why: Incisors have a thin, chisel-like incisal edge for cutting.

whyNot.0: Broad occlusal surfaces belong to premolars and molars.
whyNot.1: Two cusps is typical of a premolar; incisors have one root.
whyNot.3: Three roots is the usual upper molar pattern.

explain.body: One per quadrant, at the corner of the arch. A single pointed cusp grips and tears. They have the longest roots in the mouth (the upper canine longest of all), so they are very stable and support the corners of the lips.

test.q: Why are canines particularly stable in the jaw?
options: They are the first to erupt
test.why: Canines have the longest roots of all teeth, anchoring them firmly.

whyNot.0: Canines have one root; three roots is the upper molar pattern.
whyNot.3: Canines are not the first teeth to erupt in either dentition.

explain.body: Two per quadrant, only in the permanent dentition. Usually two cusps (bicuspids) for crushing. Usually one root, except the upper first premolar, which usually has two (buccal and palatal).

test.q: Premolars are sometimes called bicuspids. Why?
options: There are two in each arch
test.why: 'Bicuspid' means two cusps, the usual premolar pattern (buccal and lingual).

whyNot.1: Most premolars have one root; only the upper first usually has two.
whyNot.2: There are four premolars in each arch, two per quadrant.
whyNot.3: Each premolar replaces one deciduous molar.

explain.body: Three per quadrant. Broad occlusal surfaces with four or five cusps grind food. Upper molars usually have three roots (mesiobuccal, distobuccal, palatal); lower molars usually two (mesial, distal).

test.q: Which roots does a lower first molar usually have?
test.why: Lower molars usually have two roots, one mesial and one distal.

whyNot.0: Buccal and palatal roots describe an upper first premolar.
whyNot.1: These three roots describe an upper molar.
whyNot.2: A single root is typical of incisors, canines and most premolars.
